title: Module 6 Interpretation Check
intro: Each item gives you a short research situation. Decide what the evidence supports.

items.q: A researcher tests whether a program changes test scores in a population with mean 75 and sigma 12. A sample of 36 has M = 79. The z is 2.00. At alpha = .05 two-tailed, what is the decision?
o: Reject the null, since 2.00 exceeds the critical value of 1.96
Retain the null, since 2.00 is small
The decision depends on the effect size
items.why: The critical values at alpha = .05 two-tailed are plus and minus 1.96. The test statistic falls in the critical region.

items.q: For the same study, Cohen's d is the mean difference divided by sigma. What is d?
items.why: d = (79 minus 75)/12 = .33, a small to medium effect. The z of 2.00 mixes effect size with sample size.

items.q: A study fails to find a significant difference with n = 8 per group. A colleague concludes the treatment has no effect. What is the best reply?
o: The study had little power, so the result is inconclusive rather than proof of no effect
The study should have used alpha = .20
items.why: Small samples have low power. Look at the effect size and confidence interval before concluding anything.

items.q: A pharmaceutical study of 50,000 people finds a significant drop of 0.2 points on a 100 point symptom scale, an effect size near zero. What is the appropriate conclusion?
o: The effect is statistically significant but practically trivial
The result must be a Type II error
items.why: Large samples can detect minuscule effects. Significance and importance are different questions.

items.q: A researcher gets p = .06 and says, "This is nearly significant, so the effect is almost real." What is wrong?
o: The decision rule was set at .05 in advance. A result either meets it or does not, and the effect size and CI should be reported instead
The researcher should switch to a one-tailed test
items.why: Treating p values as degrees of reality blurs the logic of the test. Report the estimate and its uncertainty.
